title: All Blacks v Wallabies: Five takeaways as disciplined New Zealand run riot at Eden Park and Les Kiss suffers first defeat - Planet Rugby
content: Following a 50-19 triumph for the All Blacks over the Wallabies at Eden Park in Auckland, here’s our five takeaways from Saturday’s first Bledisloe Cup encounter. Ten minutes into this Bledisloe Cup opener, Planet Rugby was quietly cashing in its prediction chips. Australia had 90 per cent of the ball and a 7-0 lead through a lovely Tom Wright try off the lineout, whilst New Zealand had dropped a high ball, kicked a restart dead and lost a lineout to Jeremy Williams; the All Blacks were doing everything they could to lose it. Seventy minutes later the chips had been handed back, and desks around the world were reaching for re-writes as New Zealand ran in seven tries to three in a 50-19 win that ended Les Kiss‘ unbeaten start as Wallabies head coach and kept an Eden Park record Australia haven’t dented since 1986 intact. Our preview argued that New Zealand would arrive battered and bruised from four Tests against the Springboks and, rather embarrassingly, had it the wrong way round. It turns out that a month of being run over by the Bomb Squad is a fairly decent conditioning programme; those four weeks left the All Blacks hard and match-fit, the three-week break let them recharge without losing that edge, and the result was their most complete performance in a long while. It was a game of two halves; the first finished 17-14 and could have gone either way, but the second deserves framing and hanging on the wall. The hosts won it 33-5, five tries to one, with 61 per cent of the territory, scoring 26 unanswered points before Josh Nasser’s maul try gave Australia something to take to Sydney, and Will Jordan brought up the half-century at the death with his ninth try of the year. There was something fitting about the Eden Park PA reaching for Levels, by the late, great Tim Bergling, better known as Avicii, as Cam Roigard went over on 48 minutes, because plenty of players had found theirs. Roigard, Jordie Barrett, Peter Lakai and Damian McKenzie were outstanding for New Zealand, and Harry Wilson, Wright, Ben Donaldson, Rob Valetini and Williams all hit those heights in gold. Both sides wanted to run, and Andrew Brace let them get on with it, the TMO spending 70 minutes with little to do but admire the view. It came at a cost, though, with Scott Barrett failing his HIA on his return, Leroy Carter hurting his ankle as he scored and Anton Segner leaving with a head wound after a collision with a team-mate, so Dave Rennie‘s injury list grows again before Sydney. And, here’s the curious thing. Sure, Australia conceded six turnovers to New Zealand’s 13, lost only four rucks and won 92 per cent of their own lineout throws to New Zealand’s 80, but they still lost by 31 points. On the basic measures of control this was close to an even contest, and what separated the sides was how well New Zealand behaved without the ball and what they did whenever Australia made a mistake. The All Blacks were penalised for collapsing an Australian maul inside the first ten minutes and given a team warning, and from that moment they never gave Brace a reason to reach for his top pocket. Australia’s only shot at goal all night came from a not-rolling-away penalty midway through the first half, and Ryan Lonergan missed it. Put bluntly, it was the tidier side in possession that cracked; an obstruction off a lineout drive in the New Zealand 22 early in the second half wiped out Australia’s best attacking spell and will have had the coaching box reaching for something stronger than a water bottle, and their discipline fell apart in the final quarter as the tackle count mounted. New Zealand, meanwhile, fed off every Australian slip. Once Roigard found his range his box-kicking was exquisite, dropped on a sixpence so his chasers could arrive at pace and compete for the ball, and with that man Jordie Barrett and Lakai leaping into Wallaby receivers who were too often standing still, contested kicks became broken field. The first try showed exactly how; Barrett got above Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii to win Roigard’s kick, the recycle was lightning quick, and McKenzie showed and went for Lakai to finish. So, in essence, New Zealand coughed up the ball 13 times and still won by 31, because after that early warning they gave Australia almost nothing cheap from the referee and turned almost every Australian error into points. All Blacks player ratings: Damian McKenzie produces ‘statement display’ as playmaking duo ‘key’ to dominant performance McKenzie is only at ten because Rennie’s injury list currently reads like a hospital rota, but on this evidence the coach has a decision to make, both for Sydney and for next year. New Zealand repeatedly put a centre or a back-five forward at first receiver as a screen, with McKenzie hidden behind him; he arrived late and fast, and only then decided whether to take the ball to the line himself or play out the back. Australia’s defenders read the screen as the threat and set themselves for it, which meant adjusting at the last moment to a fly-half arriving at pace, and that half-second was all he needed. He beat four defenders and put Wallace Sititi and Will Jordan through, with only loose final passes stopping both breaks becoming tries. The structure works because of the man inside him. Jordie Barrett swapped into the first-receiver role cleverly all night, giving the Wallaby defence another moving part to read, and with Barrett and Roigard minding the shop, McKenzie was free to play what was in front of him rather than conduct every phase. Barrett also answered the leadership question asked of this side with Ardie Savea absent, winning contests in the air, carrying 12 times and making 16 tackles, the third-highest tally on the pitch; he carried four times in the move for Codie Taylor’s try on 54 minutes, reloading each time to clear or support again. When Richie Mo’unga and Ruben Love are fit again, Rennie will have three very different tens to choose between, and a 12 who makes the more adventurous option work. Our preview argued the last quarter would decide this Test, with Australia’s bench the weak point, but it was the third quarter that settled it; Roigard’s and Taylor’s tries took New Zealand from 17-14 to 31-14 inside 14 minutes of the restart, and the final quarter, won 19-5, decided only the margin. Australia made 200 tackles to New Zealand’s 144 and missed 30 of them, and by the second half the load was telling; they had only 39 per cent of the territory after the break, and losing Len Ikitau to an HIA early in it took the organisation out of their midfield. New Zealand’s bench then turned the screw. Kyle Preston added tempo at nine after Roigard went off, putting Josh Moorby over on the left touchline with a lovely pass. Lonergan’s intercept to stop Sititi scoring was the last real moment of Australian defiance until Nasser’s try, and the night ended with a loose pass, trying to play out from deep, bobbling free for Jordan to score. Nobody did more to hold it together than the captain. Wilson was magnificent in defeat, making 28 tackles, 11 more than anyone else on the pitch, which by the final whistle must have felt like tackling half of Auckland, and he created and finished his own try, holding Sititi at first receiver and popping to Donaldson, who went through the hole and gave it straight back to him. Wright beat five defenders and ran 76 metres, more than any other player, and between them they gave Kiss plenty to build on. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Australia can take more from this than the scoreline suggests. Their set-piece is in rude health; Williams stole two New Zealand lineouts, the scrum won all of its own ball, and Nasser’s maul try finally rewarded a drive that had come away empty twice, once to a superb goal-line stand and once to that obstruction. Two weeks after beating the Springboks in Perth, this is a reset to make in Sydney rather than a crisis to manage. Both of these sides owe a good deal of tonight to the team Australia beat in Perth. Rassie Erasmus’s Springboks, back-to-back world champions, have set a standard of physicality, set-piece precision and bench depth that everyone else in the south has had to chase, and the chasing is paying off. New Zealand have spent a month in the Springboks’ slipstream, and Australia took them on a fortnight ago and won. Erasmus has raised the bar, and his two great rivals are now playing up to it Test after Test. The wider picture is the one northern hemisphere coaches should worry about. South Africa, New Zealand and Australia are all in serious form a year out from a World Cup in Australia, and on this evidence at least, New Zealand look as complete as any of them. title: Instant analysis of Colts' Week 5 loss v. Steelers - Yahoo Sports
content: The Indianapolis Colts dropped Sunday's game against the Pittsburgh Steelers, falling to 2-3 on the season. With the clock at zero, here are our instant takeaways from the Colts' performance. - With Jaylon Carlies out, as expected, Bryce Boettcher starts next to Akeem Davis-Gaither at linebacker. - Time in the pocket and manageable down-and-distance are a recipe for Aaron Rodgers to pick apart a defense. - Missed tackles were again an issue for the Colts' defense. - Spencer Shrader continues to build upon his strong season. - Tyler Warren has been reliable all season long, but we saw him generate some chunk plays as well in this game. - It was a much cleaner performance from Daniel Jones, who didn't have any turnovers. - The Colts' passing game also found some success generating big plays, creating four plays of at least 20 yards. This has been a struggle for much of the season. - The Colts' pass rush generated only one sack and two quarterback hits. - With time in the pocket, Rodgers was efficient and able to generate some chunk plays. - Penalties were a problem, with the Colts flagged eight times. - The Colts' offense was also just 4-for-14 on third downs and 1-for-3 in the red zone. - It was a modest day for Jonathan Taylor, who totaled just 45 yards on 15 carries. title: Between madness and luxury: four differences between the Al Ahly v Zamalek clash and the Al Hilal v Al Ittihad clasico - Goal.com

Two heavyweight nights in the space of a few hours. Cairo Stadium caught fire for the Al Ahly and Zamalek summit meeting, just 24 hours after Al Hilal and Al Ittihad had served up a breathtaking clasico at Kingdom Arena. Egypt offers a historic clamour passed down through millions. Saudi Arabia offers an escalating struggle fuelled by investment and stars arriving from the biggest European leagues. Both scenes share one thing: these matches stretch far beyond three points to become a test of prestige, quality and ambition. Different circumstances, then, but the comparison between the two summit meetings throws up four clear differences: the fans, the technical level, the volume of goals and the clubs' market value. Al Ahly settled the Egyptian summit with two goals to nil. Al Hilal snatched the Riyadh clasico 3-2 in a match of five goals and swings that ran right to the final minutes. Supporters remain the element most capable of giving top-of-the-table clashes an exceptional character, but every country has its own stamp. In Cairo, the Al Ahly v Zamalek encounter sold out, with 40,000 seats handed to fans, 20,000 for each club. Both sets of fans raised banners carrying historic and patriotic messages. Al Ahly supporters celebrated the "Club of the Century" title. Zamalek's invoked the heroes of the October War, proof that the rivalry between the two giants stretches well beyond the ninety minutes. In Riyadh, the Al Hilal v Al Ittihad clasico drew 22,808 spectators according to published reports, amid a raucous atmosphere and clear competition between the stands in chanting and support. Mohammed Al-Owais added an extra touch before kick-off, walking out carrying the Gulf Cup 27 trophy as the players of both teams formed a guard of honour to celebrate Saudi Arabia's crowning as champions. The figures hand Cairo the numerical advantage, but that takes nothing away from the atmosphere in Riyadh. Fans in both cities confirm that football is not merely a game, but part of the clubs' identity and history. Between the giant banners, the chants and the songs, the stands were an essential partner in creating the spectacle. On the pitch, the clasico between Al Hilal and Al Ittihad had a clearly attacking character, thanks to the quality of the names in the forward lines and their ability to exploit space. The arrivals from the English Premier League made their mark immediately. Gabriel Martinelli, Ollie Watkins and Crysencio Summerville scored Al Hilal's three goals, confirming the rapid impact of the new signings and their ability to settle big encounters. Read also.. En-Nesyri in the dock: and the reason is Yassine Bounou! Egypt's summit took a different shape. Al Ahly managed the encounter and found Zamalek's goal at two important moments, Mohamed Hany opening the scoring in the 39th minute before Mounsef Bakrar added the second in the 80th with a superb strike from outside the penalty area. Goals were in short supply, but the decisive moments demanded concentration and ruthlessness, a trait no less important than individual skill. Neither summit held absolute technical quality over the other. The Riyadh clasico showed the value of stars capable of making the difference in open spaces, while Cairo revealed the importance of taking chances and showing pragmatism in a match charged with rivalry and pressure. In both cases, individual and collective details settled the result in favour of the more effective side. Both games packed the stands, but the goals handed the Al Hilal versus Al Ittihad clasico the edge. Five of them, in the end. Martinelli opened the scoring for Al Hilal, Youssef En-Nesyri replied for Al Ittihad, Watkins restored the lead for the Leader, Summerville added a third, and Steven Bergwijn pulled one back from the penalty spot in the 89th minute. Cairo delivered a 2-0 win for Al Ahly. Mohamed Hany struck before the break and the hosts sealed it in the closing minutes. Five goals against two, then, and the Riyadh clasico takes the spoils. That gap says more about the nature of the two matches than any absolute technical superiority. Tempo, mistakes, the chances on offer and how far each side commits bodies forward in search of a way back all shape how many goals a game produces. Still, the Saudi game served up the richer attacking fare, a comeback live right until the final moments. Al Ahly's night ran differently. They kept a clean sheet and widened the gap late, and the contest never really opened up. Add GOAL.com as a preferred source on Google to see more of our reporting The gulf widens dramatically when it comes to squad market values, based on Transfermarkt estimates for the 2026-2027 season. Al Hilal's squad is worth around 193.3 million euros and Al Ittihad's 142.55 million euros, taking the combined figure for the two Saudi clubs to roughly 335.85 million euros. Egypt's giants sit nowhere near that. Al Ahly's squad is valued at around 36.2 million euros, Zamalek's at around 16.93 million euros, a combined 53.13 million euros. That leaves Al Hilal and Al Ittihad ahead of the Cairo pair by some 282.72 million euros, almost 6.3 times the total market value of the Egyptian duo. Such numbers hand the Saudi sides a clear financial edge on paper, and the squad lists explain why. Martinelli, Watkins and Summerville have all arrived at Al Hilal from Europe's major leagues, while Al Ittihad boast a cluster of high-value professionals of their own. Market value, though, is only an estimate of what players are worth in the transfer market. It measures neither performance in a single match nor the likelihood of lifting trophies. Both showpiece fixtures, in the end, pitted two very different kinds of football magic against each other: enormous historical and popular depth in Cairo, huge investment and star names with hefty price tags in Riyadh. Al Hilal and Al Ittihad won the financial argument comfortably. The supporters and the effectiveness on the pitch still shaped how each encounter unfolded, and the two matches confirmed that football cannot be reduced to money or names alone. What counts is a team's ability to turn its potential into performance and results.

title: Devils Finish Homestand V. Sens | PREVIEW - NHL.com
content:
New Jersey conclude its a three-game homestand by hosting the Ottawa Senators Monday night at Prudential Center. Puck drop is 7:08 p.m. ET. Read below for your Game Preview presented by Flock Free Bird System Control & Services and check back for the Morning Skate Recap. NEWARK, N.J. - The Devils will hold a morning skate at 10:30 a.m. ET. Check back around noon for the lastest info and updates from that skate. The Devils power play erupted Saturday against Vancouver with three man-advantage goals, two from captain Nico Hischier. That was good for a 4-1 victory. The first goal from Hischier was the 200th of his career.  Meanwhile, goalie Jake Allen picked up the win in his 500th career NHL games. New Jersey had spurted with two losses after winning the season opener against Philadelphia in overtime. Devils defenseman Johnathan Kovacevic (knee) was removed from the Injured Reserve list and is eligible to make his season debut. With back-to-back nights for the Devils starting against Ottawa and following at Detroit, it's likely Kovacevic will play in one of the two. The biggest news of the off-season for Ottawa was trading Brady Tkachuk to Florida. Tim Stutzle has picked up the offense for Ottawa with four goals and eight points in the opening five games of the season. Drake Batherson's three goals have also contributed. On the backside, goalie Linus Ullmark is off to a remarkable start. He's allowed just five goals in four games to post a 4-0-0 record, 1.34 goals-against average and 942 save percentage. The Devils captain scored two goals, both on the power play, against Vancouver. He added an assist for a three-point night. Ottawa's Tim Stutzle has been a one-man wrecking machine in the offensive zone. He's posted four goals, four assists and eight points in the opening five games. That includes one three-point game and three multi-point games. title: Triple-Black 1971 Plymouth Cuda Packs Rare V-Code and 4-Speed Combo - autoevolution
content:
These two years were the only seasons when the Barracuda was available with Mopar's greatest high-performance engines. I'm obviously talking about the 426-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) Hemi and the 440-cubic-inch (7.2-liter) Six-Barrel V8s. Both mills are quite sought-after today. But they're also rare, mainly because they were ordered in low quantities due to high insurance rates. How rare, do you ask? Well, Plymouth sold only 666 Hemi-equipped Cudas in 1970. The Six-Barrel powerplant found 1,784 buyers that year. The numbers are naturally much smaller in 1971. Only 114 Cudas rolled off the assembly line with the 426 Hemi, and only 254 examples were ordered with the 440 Six-Barrel. The Hemi Cuda convertible is particularly scarce, with only seven produced, and pretty much the only version valued at over $2 million. But I'm actually here to talk about the 1971 Six-Barrel model. It's a bit more common and won't fetch a seven-figure sum, but it's one of those Mopar you don't see very often. And the fact that one is about to go under the hammer at Mecum's Dallas/Fort Worth 2026 auction this October is a pretty big deal. As I previously mention, Plymouth produced only 254 units equipped with this engine. The Mopar you see here is a hardtop, which makes it one of 237 Six-Barrel cars in this body style. But we also need to factor in the four-speed manual transmission. Existing records show that only 108 hardtops also got this gearbox. The drivetrain is enough to make this Cuda highly desirable, but this muscle car has another cool thing going on for it: it's a triple-black classic. I know some argue that a hardtop needs a vinyl top in order to be a true triple-black car, but the metal top is black, so this Cuda is as sinister as they get. And if you're a fan of subtle details, it also has the rare billboard decals in matte black. I'd be willing to bet that the color combo makes it a one-of-a-kind gem with this drivetrain, but I don't have any paperwork to prove it. Even so, it's very much a holy-grail unit when it comes to Six-Barrel Plymouths. And it obviously has all the desirable period-correct features, including the pistol-grip shifter, Shaker hood, and Rallye instrument cluster. The rear spoiler is also a rare sight. The add doesn't specifically mention whether the engine is numbers-matching but lists a Super Track Pak rear end with a Dana 60 axle with 4.10 gears. This Mopar will be at home on the drag strip, should you decide to put its 390-horsepower V8 to good use on Sundays. Likewise, there is no info on whether this car was restored or whether the 34,349-mile (55,279-km) reading on the odometer is true. But the car comes with a broadcast sheet that confirms all of its features and options. The Mopar will go under the hammer on October 24, and it should change hands for well over $100,000. But I wouldn't be surprised to see it fetch more than $200,000. Ask Ciprian about cars and he'll reveal an obsession with classics and an annoyance with modern design cues. (NYSE:V) operates a global payments network, earning fees from payment volumes, transaction processing, and related services. Banks issue cards and extend credit; the company connects financial institutions and merchants without funding consumers' card balances. Digital commerce and international spending expand that opportunity, but banks and merchants want a share of the growth. The company appears in Insider Monkey's 10 Most Profitable Blue Chip Stocks to Buy According to Hedge Funds. The investment question is whether its network retains enough profit after client rebates to justify the earnings multiple. Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) benefits when wider acceptance makes its network more useful to cardholders, attracting additional banks and merchants. Reliability, fraud controls and established integrations reinforce that advantage. New payment channels create value when they expand profitable activity, the same distinction as when a new checkout channel adds payment revenue. Fiscal Q3 2026 processed transactions increased 10%, while cross-border volume excluding transactions within Europe grew 12% in constant dollars. Value-added services generated $3.8 billion of revenue. Security, acceptance and advisory tools can deepen relationships and improve revenue per customer. Maintaining that advantage requires technology, personnel and marketing spending. Competing networks and direct bank-payment options can strengthen clients' bargaining power. Incentives create value when the additional revenue they secure covers both concessions and associated operating costs, leaving an adequate profit. Network scale supports a premium only when those relationships produce profitable repeat business. Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) carries approximately 26x forward P/E and 33x trailing P/E. Trailing P/E uses historical reported earnings; forward P/E uses forecast earnings. The forward valuation looks fair given sustained transaction growth and strong profitability, provided client concessions and operating costs leave enough room for earnings to compound. Analysts expect adjusted EPS of approximately $15.00 in fiscal 2027, ending September, versus $13.23 for fiscal 2026, implying 13% growth. Expected revenue growth of approximately 11% supplies much of the operating foundation. Additional services, pricing, and share repurchases can help EPS grow faster than sales. Reported earnings and adjusted forecasts also use different accounting treatments. Q3 reported EPS was $2.97, versus non-GAAP adjusted EPS of $3.32. Severance and certain litigation provisions explain most of that gap. The $563 million severance charge depressed reported earnings, while management plans to reinvest workforce savings in growth opportunities. Its disappearance could improve a future GAAP comparison. Because adjusted earnings already exclude that charge, forecast growth in adjusted EPS must come from improvements elsewhere. Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) reported 17% growth in non-GAAP operating expenses in Q3, exceeding 14% net-revenue growth. Some personnel-expense growth reflected deferred-compensation remeasurement offset by investment income, so that component did not reduce EPS. Marketing, technology, and employee spending still require productive returns, illustrating why faster payments do not automatically produce wider margins. Buybacks also contributed: adjusted net income increased 8%, while adjusted EPS rose 11%. Reducing the share count can support per-share growth, but requires cash that also funds client contracts and reinvestment. The current 26x forward P/E for Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) compares with approximately 26x on September 19, 2024, and 27x at its September 2025 fiscal year-end. Investors are paying roughly the same multiple as in the earlier observation and modestly less than at the later year-end. That offers little evidence of a substantial historical bargain. Adjusted EPS grew 15% in fiscal 2024 and 14% in 2025. The 13% growth forecast for 2027 supports a broadly similar valuation, while stronger cash conversion would be needed to make a higher multiple compelling. The operating demands behind today's valuation deserve attention. Client incentives increased 14% against 17% net-revenue growth in fiscal Q2 2026. In Q3, those rates became 18% and 14%. Management attributed faster incentive growth partly to unusually low growth in the prior-year comparison and stronger client performance. It expected Q4 incentive growth slightly above Q3 as renewals and new business added costs. Incentives are already deducted from net revenue. Measured against revenue before those deductions, they absorbed approximately 28.7% in Q3, versus 28.1% a year earlier. About one-third of incremental revenue before incentives went into additional concessions. Across nine months, however, the proportion remained approximately 28.1%, versus 28.2%. The longer period supports the existing valuation, while the quarterly deterioration helps explain why a return to a higher multiple needs stronger evidence. The test remains how much loyalty is worth after customers receive their rewards. Cash generation adds another requirement for Visa Inc. (NYSE:V). Subtracting $1.18 billion of capital expenditure from nine-month operating cash flow of $16.34 billion leaves approximately $15.16 billion, down from $15.73 billion. Higher litigation and incentive payments, alongside tax-payment timing, contributed to the decline. Upfront incentives can consume cash before being recognized against revenue, so contract growth must eventually replenish the cash committed to winning it. Mastercard Incorporated (NYSE:MA) is the closest operating peer because both companies earn network fees and sell related services without directly financing cardholder balances. Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) and Mastercard Incorporated (NYSE:MA) both carry approximately 26x forward P/E. For the same calendar quarter ending December 2026, analysts expect adjusted EPS growth of approximately 14% and 9%, respectively. That is fiscal Q1 2027 for the primary company and Q4 2026 for the peer. Faster expected near-term growth supports the similar multiples, although ongoing profitability matters beyond that quarter. For the June quarter, the primary company's calculated adjusted operating margin was 66.7%, down from 67.5%. The peer's adjusted margin rose to 61.1% from 59.9%, as 14% revenue growth outpaced 11% adjusted expense growth. The primary company retains the higher adjusted margin; the peer shows the stronger recent margin trend. Customer bargaining power affects both networks. The peer's payment-network rebates and incentives rose 22%, reflecting transaction growth and new or renewed contracts. Its improving margin shows that larger concessions can coexist with profitable expansion when services and operating efficiency compensate. Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) also had approximately $11.5 billion of borrowings less cash and cash equivalents in June, versus $13.4 billion for the peer. Its larger quarterly operating-profit base and lower net debt provide more financial room. That supports the similar multiple, while renewed cash growth would strengthen the case more than another increase in buybacks. Read more: 10 Most Promising Fintech Stocks to Buy Now Visa Inc. (NYSE:V) is fairly valued at approximately 26x forward earnings if profitable payment volumes and additional services deliver the expected earnings growth. Its network supports that assessment, while the historical comparison offers only a modest discount to 2025. Sustaining the valuation requires profitable transaction growth after incentives, operating expenses that leave more revenue for shareholders, and stronger cash generation after investment. If concessions keep absorbing more incremental revenue while cash conversion weakens, the same multiple would become harder to justify. title: Liverpool v Man City player ratings: Florian Wirtz has tough game for Reds - BBC
content: Highlights: Manchester City beat Liverpool to extend perfect start Erling Haaland, Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki scored as Manchester City inflicted a first defeat for Liverpool on Andoni Iraola. Premier League: Man City cruise to statement win at 10-man Liverpool - reaction Alisson: Could do nothing to keep out Erling Haaland's strike then beaten by a beauty from Jeremy Doku and some solid footwork from Rayan Cherki. 5 Ronald Araujo: Got a cheap yellow card early on and will be annoyed that the first two Man City goals came from his side. 5 Virgil van Dijk: Often pushed out of position to help Liverpool deal with getting outnumbered in midfield. Perhaps could have closed Haaland down quicker. 6 Jeremy Jacquet: Wasn't a bad display from a young talent who is very impressive but this must have been a real eye-opener against a quality City attack. 6 Milos Kerkez: Battled well with Iliman Ndiaye and pushed up regularly but lacked  quality in the final third. 5 Alexis Mac Allister: Grew into the game and put in a good shift but struggled once Liverpool went down to 10 men. 5 Ryan Gravenberch: Came in for the injured Dominik Szoboszlai and was Liverpool's best player until he got sent off for a second yellow card. title: How Much It Costs To Replace A Honda CR-V Hybrid Battery - SlashGear
content: Honda added a hybrid powertrain to its popular compact SUV back in 2020. Hybrid powertrains are great for fuel efficiency, and the company is promising EPA estimates of up to 43 mpg city and 36 mpg combined on the 2026 CR-V. However, the hybrid battery in your car won't last forever. Which brings us to the question: how much will it cost to replace the hybrid battery on your CR-V? According to estimates from select Honda dealerships, replacing the hybrid battery of the CR-V costs anywhere between $2,000 and $7,000. That's because the CR-V uses a lithium-ion battery pack, which is slightly more expensive to replace than the nickel-metal-hydride pack used in earlier Honda Civic, Insight, and Accord hybrids. The actual cost of replacing your CR-V's hybrid battery depends on different factors, such as the cost of labor. One 2023 Honda CR-V owner says they were asked to pay $5,000 by a Honda dealership to replace the hybrid battery. If you were to get the hybrid battery pack alone, the cost varies depending on the model year of your car. Honda sells the battery pack for the 2025 Honda CR-V Hybrid for $3,515 through its official store. On the other hand, a remanufactured battery pack for the 2022 CR-V is listed for $5,346. However, these battery packs include all the auxiliary parts like the casing, which you may not need if the one in your CR-V is in good condition. Also, this is the part cost alone, so when you factor in taxes, labor, and other necessary charges, it'll fall within the range quoted by different Honda dealerships. Replacing the hybrid battery on a CR-V sure isn't cheap, especially if you're paying out of pocket. And, as reports suggest, Honda could make the hybrid powertrain standard on the CR-V in the future. So if you have to replace the hybrid battery often, keeping the CR-V on the road can get expensive. However, you might not need to replace the battery anytime soon after you drive off the lot with your new hybrid Honda CR-V. According to estimates published on Honda's U.K. website, a typical hybrid battery should last between six and 10 years for the average driver. However, how fast the battery pack in your CR-V degrades depends on different factors because it's a consumable part. Driving and maintenance habits can also affect how long your hybrid battery lasts, so your mileage will vary. The good news is that Honda offers a hybrid battery warranty that covers your first years of ownership. Dubbed the High Voltage Battery Capacity Warranty, it covers pack degradation if it falls below 75% of its original capacity within the first eight years or 100,000 miles (whichever comes first). If it happens within the warranty period, Honda will either repair the battery pack or replace it at no cost. The warranty period also suggests the company is confident you likely won't need to replace the hybrid battery before eight years have passed or you reach 100,000 miles. Battery degradation is normal. As you continue to use your CR-V, the battery health will slowly decline. However, before your Honda CR-V hybrid battery completely fails and needs a replacement or repair, there are certain signs that your vehicle will show. If you see any of them, then beware that you might need to take your CR-V to a dealership for repair. The first, and perhaps the most obvious sign that you'll see, is a decline in fuel economy. If everything else stays the same, including your driving style, but the CR-V suddenly uses more fuel than it used to, it may indicate a weakening hybrid battery. A second sign is the IMA warning light on your dashboard or a hybrid battery warning light (a battery icon with an exclamation mark). Hybrid battery issues can also trigger the check engine light, either on its own or alongside the IMA or hybrid battery warning light. You may also see a charge gauge rising and falling rapidly. That indicates the battery pack is worn out and can't hold electric charge for long, which is one of the common problems with hybrid batteries. You might also experience a reduction in electric assist, with the gas engine engaging more often than it used to. Your CR-V might also not engage the battery alone, which could mean the battery no longer has enough capacity to power the vehicle. Lastly, you might hear the battery cooling fan running more loudly or frequently than it used to. These signs aren't necessarily an indication that you need to replace your hybrid battery because they might overlap with other issues. However, once you notice any of them, it's a good idea to take your CR-V in for a full diagnosis to help pinpoint the problem.

title: NFL today: How to watch 49ers v Seahawks, TV channels & live stream Sunday 11 October - The Guardian
content: How will the Seahawks and 49ers fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options Last winter, two games between the 49ers and Seahawks decided the shape of the NFL season. The two teams played each other in the Bay Area on the last weekend of the regular season, and Seattle’s win secured the NFC West and homefield advantage when the teams met later in the NFC divisional playoffs. Seattle’s advantage only got more lopsided at home, and a 41-6 win proved to be the launching pad that sent the Seahawks flying through the rest of the playoffs, ending with a Super Bowl victory. The Niners watched from home. Now they meet again in one of the most anticipated games of the 2026 season to date. The 49ers take an unbeaten record on the road against a 3-1 Seattle team who have kept the train on the tracks despite Sam Darnold getting hurt early in Week 1 and missing a game. Whoever wins here will claim divisional favorite status as we move into the second quarter of the season, and they’ll also give themselves a good shot to claim a head-to-head tiebreaker that may be important in the league’s most competitive division. United States: Watch on Fox or stream on Fox One or Fubo (where the local Fox affiliate carries the game). United Kingdom: Watch on Sky Sports NFL or stream on NOW The main man to watch for Seattle is the same as ever: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who just had one of the handful of most productive receiving seasons ever and is so far averaging more yards per game (120) than he did when he won Offensive Player of the Year. The Seahawks do not have a clear No 2 wideout and have some running back problems, too, given that Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker now plays for the Chiefs and first-round rookie Jadarian Price went to injured reserve this week. But as long as an offense has JSN, it has a chance to put up serious point totals. The Seahawks’ 105 points in four games are tied for sixth in the NFC. They’ll rise up the ranks if non-JSN contributors emerge. The 49ers are a more balanced juggernaut at the moment. Brock Purdy continues to be Brock Purdy, putting up terrific numbers in a maximally supportive system. A large handful of offensive players on the wrong side of 30 have all maintained their access to the fountain of youth: Trent Williams blocking, Christian McCaffrey running and catching, and Mike Evans, George Kittle, and Deebo Samuel as downfield targets. An injured defensive front (currently missing star edge rusher Nick Bosa and tackle James Thompson) has not stopped the 49ers’ defense from giving up the third-fewest yards per play in the NFL. The only trouble is that the two teams ahead of them are the Seahawks and Rams. Will this division put three teams in the playoff again? It looks that way.

content: Coventry celebrated their first Premier League goal and points for more than 25 years by beating Nottingham Forest before the international break. The caveat to Coventry's run of four straight league defeats from the start of the season was that it included away games against last season's top two sides. In a more favourable-looking run this month, they have three home fixtures out of four and will face the two teams who sat below them going into the latest round of matches. Having felled Forest, Coventry are attempting to become the first English side in 127 years to earn consecutive top-flight wins immediately after losing their opening four games without scoring. Derby County are the only club to do so, in 1899, and they rallied to finish sixth. A far more modern precedent to give Coventry some belief is that three promoted sides have started as badly as them in the Premier League and still avoided relegation. Head coach Frank Lampard hopes his team can take inspiration from the memory of their most recent Monday night home game, an outstanding 3-1 win over Middlesbrough in February. Coventry were second to Boro going into that fixture after losing a 10-point lead, but victory put them back on top and they pulled away to clinch the Championship title. "I watch parts of that game back regularly because it was our outstanding game last year considering what was on it," said Lampard. "And now we have to do 38 (sic) versions of that kind of feeling to get things nailed on." Newcastle are playing promoted opponents for the second match in a row, having held off a late fightback to end Hull City's unbeaten start to the season. That result, coupled with a high-tempo first-half display, made partial amends for the dismal 4-1 defeat at Leeds United five days earlier. Newcastle's defensive vulnerability is clear; they faced a league-high 97 shots across their opening five games. Nonetheless, a tally of eight points from five games is a solid start under Matthias Jaissle – especially in the wake of a tumultuous summer during which they sold their three highest-profile players. Despite injuries hindering Newcastle's youthful rebuild, a win on Monday would give Jaissle the joint-second best start by a Magpies manager after six Premier League games.
